new_statements.quote: 2.5.1. Rhythmic stress. Tiriyó phonological words follow a pattern of alternation between non-prominent (unstressed) and prominent (stressed) syllables. If the phonological word is composed exclusively of (C)V syllables, then every second syllable from the beginning of the word will be stressed, except for the last syllable, which is always unstressed. [p. 60] ... The following rules summarize the various facts described above ... (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. [p. 63]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tiriyó (Trio) has iambic rhythmic stress over the phonological word: light (C)V syllables are parsed left to right with stress on every second one, heavy syllables ((C)Vh, (C)VN, (C)VV etc.) are always stressed when non-final and restart the count, and the word-final syllable is never stressed; stressed light syllables surface with vowel length. Adding syllabic prefixes shifts stress accordingly.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction established: 'aside from an impression that the last stressed syllable in a phonological word sounds stronger than the others, there seems to be no reason to analyze any single syllable in a phonological word as bearing primary stress' (p. 71). All rhythmic beats are treated as equal stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: All-(C)V words of one or two syllables receive no true stress (pitch drop from first to second syllable, no lengthening, optional gemination of a medial stop), p. 66-67; initial underlying VV or other heavy syllables in disyllables keep length/stress under affixation (p. 67); phonetic correlate is length, high pitch is intonational not stress (p. 70); two dialects (h- vs. non-h) differ in what counts as heavy (§2.4.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (word plus clitics, e.g. /maja_ton/ [majá:ton]); examples are citation forms and inflected verbs; intonation (utterance domain) is superimposed and can alter pitch on stressed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: salu1254 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping (spurious) languoid. Glottolog's comment (saved): the only two wordlists bearing this name in the stated area are 'clearly Trio [tri]' (citing Carlin 2004: 8), i.e. trio1238 Trió/Tiriyó; alternatively, if 'Salumá' means the group Frikel (1957) calls Charúma (his Stammesregister no. 19 gives 'Tcharúma; Tsaníma; bei den Aparai und Wáyana: Sarúma, Salúma', assigned to his 'Parukotó-Charúma' dialect group), the language is Waiwai (waiw1244), which is already in the catalog from Hawkins 1998. The stress statement quoted below is Meira's for Tiriyó/Trio (trio1238), the language the 'Salumá' wordlists actually attest; it must not be entered as a separate Salumá record (a retired code does not make a separate language; trio1238 is its own target in our source list).

sources.note: §2.5.1 pp. 60-71: iambic rhythmic stress in the phonological word: final syllable never stressed; every non-final heavy (non-(C)V) syllable stressed; every second light syllable counting from word start or nearest heavy syllable stressed; correlate is vowel length, not pitch; no clear primary stress (impression that the last stressed syllable is strongest); all-light disyllables get no true stress.
